qs.q: During the final stages of the coagulation cascade, a specific plasma enzyme solidifies the provisional platelet plug by forming covalent bonds between adjacent monomers. What is the primary function of this enzyme?
o: Acting as a cofactor for Factor Xa
qs.e: Factor XIII is the fibrin-stabilising factor that cross-links fibrin monomers into a stable, insoluble fibrin clot. Factor XII initiates the intrinsic contact activation pathway.
qs.s: Haemostasis & Coagulation: Platelet Function & Bleeding Disorders: MCQs

qs.q: A researcher is studying physiologic negative feedback mechanisms in the coagulation cascade. Which of the following describes the primary action of tissue factor pathway inhibitor?
o: Stimulation of tissue plasminogen activator release
Cleavage and inactivation of factors Va and VIIIa
Inhibition of the factor VIIa-tissue factor complex
qs.e: TFPI directly inhibits the factor VIIa-tissue factor complex to limit extrinsic pathway activity. Inactivation of factors Va and VIIIa is instead performed by activated protein C.
qs.s: Haemostasis & Coagulation: Platelet Function & Bleeding Disorders: MCQs

qs.q: During the coagulation cascade, soluble fibrinogen is converted into which insoluble protein to stabilize the platelet plug?
qs.e: Coagulation involves converting soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, creating a mesh that stabilizes the plug. Thrombin acts as an enzyme in this conversion rather than forming the structural mesh itself.

qs.q: End product of the coagulation cascade?
qs.e: Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen → fibrin monomers → polymerize → cross-linked by Factor XIIIa into a stable insoluble clot.
qs.s: Haemostasis MCQs: Master Coagulation & Bleeding Control

qs.q: What is the end product of the coagulation cascade? ---
o: Formation of an insoluble fibrin clot
qs.e: The coagulation cascade ultimately converts soluble fibrinogen into an insoluble fibrin network that stabilizes the platelet plug.

qs.q: The coagulation cascade's final common pathway begins with activation of
qs.e: Factor Xa combines with Factor Va (prothrombinase complex) to convert prothrombin to thrombin — the start of the common pathway.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: The coagulation cascade is a series of enzymatic steps that convert fibrinogen to fibrin, stabilising a platelet plug into a durable clot. It is tightly regulated to balance bleeding and thrombosis, and failure leads to life‑threatening bleeding or clotting disorders.

sections.p: Coagulation is the body’s emergency repair system. When a vessel is injured, platelets adhere and release factors that activate a cascade of clotting proteins, ultimately forming a fibrin mesh that seals the wound.
b: Balance prevents excessive bleeding or clotting

sections.p: The cascade has two converging pathways: intrinsic (contact activation) and extrinsic (tissue factor). Both lead to factor X activation, generating thrombin, which converts fibrinogen to fibrin and amplifies the response.
b: Intrinsic: Factor XII → XI → IX → VIII → X

t.b: Measures extrinsic pathway function; prolonged PT suggests vitamin K deficiency, warfarin effect, or liver disease.
Assesses intrinsic pathway; prolonged aPTT indicates factor XII, XI, IX, VIII deficiencies or lupus anticoagulant.
Low fibrinogen indicates consumption (DIC) or liver failure; high may suggest inflammation.
Elevated in active clot breakdown; used to rule out thrombosis but can be high in infection or trauma.

sections.p: Natural anticoagulants (protein C, protein S, antithrombin) and fibrinolysis (tPA) keep clot size appropriate. Endothelial cells release prostacyclin and nitric oxide to inhibit platelet aggregation.
b: Protein C/S deactivate factors Va and VIIIa
Antithrombin inhibits thrombin and factor Xa
tPA converts plasminogen to plasmin, dissolving fibrin

t.b: Low activity indicates inherited or acquired thrombophilia; high activity may be seen in sepsis.
Low antithrombin predisposes to thrombosis; replacement used in severe deficiency.

sections.p: Deficiencies of clotting factors, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, sepsis, or trauma can cause bleeding. Overactivation leads to thrombosis or DIC, where widespread clotting consumes factors and causes bleeding.

t.b: High INR indicates anticoagulation or liver failure.
Low platelets suggest consumption or marrow suppression.
Prolonged in factor VIII/IX deficiency or lupus anticoagulant.

sections.p: Coagulation tests guide anticoagulant therapy, evaluate bleeding risk before surgery, and diagnose conditions like DIC, hemophilia, and liver disease. In low‑resource settings, point‑of‑care tests and clinical scoring are vital.

t.b: Assesses platelet function; prolonged in platelet disorders.
Provides real‑time clot formation dynamics; useful when lab access is limited.

sections.p: Remember the two pathways converge on factor X. A prolonged PT with normal aPTT points to the extrinsic pathway. In DIC, both PT and aPTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low, and D‑dimer is high.
b: DIC: prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D‑dimer

whenToSeekHelp: Severe uncontrolled bleeding, sudden onset of shortness of breath with chest pain (possible pulmonary embolism), sudden neurological deficit (stroke), massive hemoptysis

faq.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary haemostasis?
faq.a: Primary haemostasis is platelet plug formation; secondary haemostasis is the coagulation cascade that stabilises the plug with fibrin.

faq.q: Why does warfarin increase PT but not aPTT?
faq.a: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K–dependent factors II, VII, IX, X; factor VII (extrinsic pathway) is most sensitive, raising PT.

faq.q: Can a normal platelet count rule out bleeding disorders?
faq.a: No; platelet function defects can cause bleeding even with normal counts, so functional tests may be needed.
